beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: The pitch is not 'roll out the agent to everyone', and that is an unusually modest claim.

beats.trigger: **Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.**
beats.got: I have a dozen of these. The telco's learning portal alone would do.

beats.trigger: **Test** the switch assumptions and name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack
beats.got: There are four things you could hand a colleague, and I don't know what a `memory/` folder is.

beats.trigger: Your agent, skill, output or interface is a candidate for hire: does it do the job better than what they currently use?
beats.got: Jobs-to-be-Done, which I know. It is an old frame applied to agents, and a sensible one.

beats.trigger: If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.
beats.got: The agent reads my files and drafts a profile of a teammate, and I'm supposed to check whether it's generic. That check is useful.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is not on the list.
beats.got: Four concrete ways to share, and they say outright that the obvious fifth option doesn't work. I'd call that candid.

beats.trigger: turns it into a technical plan plus a people plan
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Next step is more planning files.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: There is a test for whether you found the real obstacle or only the first one. That beats most workshop advice I've had.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: Engineers always write a good technical plan and leave the people half empty. They've said it out loud.

beats.trigger: writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are called hypotheses, not answers. That's a more honest framing than the last programmes used.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: Ask what would make them switch, not how to get them to adopt. It's a good question and I can reuse it with no AI involved.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A premortem. It's a known technique, and a pessimistic one, so I like it.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Picking a tool because it fits the platform is shopping. That is exactly what happened in the last three transformations.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Licence counts are reported as if they measured adoption, and they don't. I've sat in those steering groups.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: The trainer admits a project of his own stalled, and the cause was leadership attention, not the technology. That is my Tuesday.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: You can copy the agent's context, limits and checks, but not the person who answers for it.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each of the four sharing options asks something different of the receiver.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The rival is the spreadsheet and the gut call, not another tool.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building anything else. That's cheap and I can test it myself.

beats.trigger: It is rarely the same person across all four.
beats.got: Different colleagues need different sharing options. Fair enough.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: The plan counts as a guess until one person has answered, and that is how I would run it too.

beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Access is not adoption. A licence rollout tells you nothing about whether anyone changed how they work.
Ask 'what would have to be true for them to switch?' before pushing a tool. I can use that question on any change, AI or not.
A plan with a technical half and an empty people half is not finished.

monday.move: Pick one team in my unit that got a tool and doesn't use it. Ask one person how they do that job today and what they'd have to see to switch.
monday.who: One person on my team, probably someone from the licence rollout that stalled
monday.when: Tuesday or Wednesday, between steering groups
monday.stop_condition: If the answer is only 'no time', I drop the AI angle and treat it as a workload problem
monday.blocker: My calendar full of the last programme's steering groups, and that I haven't seen an agent do anything I couldn't get otherwise

misconception.why: The module never argued about whether this blows over. The access-versus-adoption point is what I'd say about every earlier transformation, so it confirms my scepticism more than it challenges it. I did not see a demo of something that would not have been possible two years ago.

one_line: Honest and reusable, mostly a method for switching behaviour with little new about the technology, though the story about the stalled decision is true to life.
